building.name: Sacred Heart Church
building.completed_conflict: The assessor's roll gives 1900; the church was dedicated in 1898 and finished in 1909.

historical_record.description: The first pastor of Sacred Heart parish, founded the year before, bought the core of this property at the corner of Fillmore and Fell Streets and moved the parish's first home onto it — a derelict one-storey Methodist chapel from the corner of Linden and Buchanan Streets. A further lot on Fell Street, bought in 1889, completed the church's frontage as it stands.

Sacred Heart Church, Thomas J. Welsh's buff pressed-brick Romanesque Revival church, was dedicated by Archbishop Riordan, its cornerstone having been laid on 7 September 1897. Money ran out with only 126 feet of the planned 169-foot nave built, and a temporary wooden wall closed the east end; the parish then counted 1,800 families.

The church was finished to Welsh & Carey's original plans and rededicated: George Goodman built the rest of the nave, the transepts with their rose windows, the sanctuary, the sacristies and a large above-ground basement hall, work begun in 1905 and stopped by the earthquake after the foundations went in, and the sanctuary was reinforced that year to carry 55 tons of marble altars.
A Hook & Hastings pipe organ was installed.
The sacristy was enlarged, the altar and the back of the sanctuary remodelled, and a new baptistery built with new stairs to the choir loft.

Father Eugene Boyle, the Catholic civil-rights activist, became pastor and until 1972 made the parish a centre of activism in the Western Addition — opening it to Vietnam Veterans Against the War, who had an office here, to conscientious objectors and to the student groups behind the San Francisco State strike, and turning the parish school into a community school.

The Black Panther Party's Breakfast Program for Children opened in the church's basement hall and kitchen, feeding 75 to 100 children a day. The coloring books depicting police as pigs, which the police told a Senate committee that year were being handed out here, were shown in 1975 to have been planted in the basement by the FBI.

The United Farm Workers' Bay Area lettuce boycott was launched here: about 500 farm workers met at Sacred Heart three days after the boycott was announced on 17 September, with a mass and a sermon by Father Boyle, a press conference and a march, and the boycott kept its first local headquarters in the parish.

After the Loma Prieta earthquake black safety netting was hung under the nave ceiling to catch falling plaster; the damage, and the cost of a seismic retrofit, put the parish on the Archdiocese's closure list from 1993.

The Archdiocese closed Sacred Heart Church at the end of the year, citing the cost of earthquake repair and a shrinking congregation, and most parishioners moved to St. Boniface in the Tenderloin; the parish school had already been merged with St. Dominic's in 2003.

A wide opening was cut into the basement of the north transept and the basement gutted for a parking garage, after the altars, the transepts' rose-window glass, the pews, the organ and other fittings had been removed between 2009 and 2015.

The church, rectory, school and convent were listed together on the National Register of Historic Places as the Sacred Heart Parish Complex: for the growth of the Catholic Western Addition, for Father Eugene Boyle's civil-rights ministry, and as a Romanesque Revival parish group whose church is Thomas J. Welsh's only surviving Romanesque Revival building.
